en: Having prostrated before the divine seer Atharvan, who bears the head of a horse, I shall fully expound the detailed procedure for the dental-labial [consonants]. 1.1.
When the study of the Veda has commenced, a doubt constantly arises among the learned and the wise regarding the letter *ba*: "Is it labial (*auṣṭhya*) or dental (*dantya*)? (1.2)

Therefore, for the sake of determining their rules and for cutting through doubt, I have already explained those beginning with the dentals; now I shall describe those beginning with the labials in their proper order. 1.3.

Furthermore, wherever these [qualities] might be seen, even in an inanimate object, the wise man perceives therein the quality of heat (*auṣṭya*), just as one who is afraid perceives [heat] in those who carry it. 1.4.

In the case of the words *bala*, *bāṇa*, and *bila*, when they are accented on the first syllable, as well as when they are compounded, that which is accented on the final syllable is distinguished [as the correct form]. (1.5)
Balada, Abala, Anugrahābala, and Dhanvan, as well as Balāsa and Bāhu—these are the teachers in all the grammatical cases. 1.6.
May Bali with his strength, Barhis with his lack of strength, Bradhna, Kiltviṣa, Ketu, and Kumba overcome the powerful one with the cry "bāliti. // 1.7 //
The words *bāhuṃ*, *bohi*, *baṃdhuḥ*, *bahubādhe*, and *bṛhat*—as well as *yat*, *pibati*, and *bruvate*—are proclaimed to be used according to their actual meanings. (1.8)
The inhabitants of Bāsta [are known] by their arm-marks, as well as by the strength of their arms;
many are the Kābavas on the arms, and likewise, O Bodha, there are many Bahvas.
Likewise, the *badhnya*, the *tāluva*, and the *bahvī* are proclaimed as the ninth;
indeed, all these are considered to be the first to be touched among all sounds. (1.10)
Vaibādha and Devabandhu are [the names] for Vibaddha; however, Vibandhu is used among the Vibandhus.
The second [name], Sparśya, is to be known as applicable likewise in the case of Vibabādha.
*bāhu*, *bāhavaḥ*, *bahulam*, *budhnyam*, and *baddhakam*—all these are labials; those not mentioned here, however, are dentals. (1.12)
Thus ends the first chapter.
One should touch [the teeth] with the tips of the teeth from the lower part to the upper part, section by section; however, one should not apply pressure that causes pain. 2.1.
You are the woolen blanket, the *balbaja* grass, the seed, the climbing vine, and the *brahmāṃ*. O *biṣkala*, you are the *barjahya*; O *śabala*, you have pierced through the birds. 2.2.
Bahiṣṭha, Budhnya, Paḍbīśa, Arbuda, Badhira, Ābayobindu, Saṃbiṃba, Kāhābā, and Udumbara. (2.3)
Kubera covered the ground with heaps of beautiful, strong, conch-like ivory and with brown,
pillar-shaped objects that resounded with a drum-like beat.
In the unconfined, through non-obstruction, you have bound the Buddhas born from the lineage; alas, alas! You are the kinsman, the lotus-stalk, the eunuch, and the one who conquers in the waters.
Badha bound Prabandhya and Ulbana, as well as Kaberaka; Ailaba besieged [them], and the Balhikas also laid siege. (2.6)
May there be awakening through the Bṛhatsāman; likewise may there be awakening through sound.
Wherever there may be a remaining bond, may there be for me the binding of sleep.
When *alābu*, *baja*, and *bāṇa* have the acute accent on their first syllable, they mean "arrow";
however, the wise know that the word *brahma* with the labial [vowel *u*] signifies all things. (2.8)
In the *chubuka* year, in *bāla*, in *keśabāla*, and likewise in *adhibāla*, youth is said [to be defined]; in the remaining [years], it is determined by its measure.
Bibheda was among the first, as were Bheda and Paribala; likewise Bandhula, Sindhura, and another named Bala—wherever these were found. (2.10)
Tuchabda, Cubuka, Babhūvu, and Babhūvuṣī—all these, having abandoned their kin, devoured one another. 2.11.
Thus ends the second chapter.
The procedure for the dentals and labials is completed.
